problem: Learning-based visual navigators such as RECON, ViNG, BC and PPO use uninformed exploration or short-horizon control. They cannot reach goals hundreds of meters to kilometers away in unseen outdoor environments. Classical methods instead need accurate geometric maps or localization, and cannot exploit noisy, schematic side information like roadmaps, satellite images or approximate GPS.
motivation: Humans navigate new areas with rough 'mental maps' and paper maps rather than accurate geometric reconstructions. Geographic hints are widely available (GPS accurate to about 2-5 m, roadmaps, satellite images) but outdated or inaccurate. A robot should use such hints to bias long-range search while still relying on learned egocentric traversability for control, so that it stays robust when the hints are wrong.
key_idea: Combine a learned image-based latent goal model (local reachability, actions and GPS offsets of sampled subgoals) with a contrastively learned heuristic that reads overhead maps. These drive an A*-like physical search (ViKiNG-A*) over an incrementally built topological graph, with the map used only as a heuristic.
insight: Decoupling hints (used only in the high-level heuristic) from control (egocentric images only) lets the system benefit from maps when they are useful and stay robust when they are not. With outdated satellite images (a truck added), the local model proposes only collision-free subgoals and the robot re-routes. With a map offset by about 5 km, it follows 'phantom' road curvature but still succeeds. The Fig. 12 ablation shows the heuristic matters: GPS-only (ℓ2 heuristic) reaches the goal but takes 0.73 km / 17:20 versus 0.31 km / 06:40 with satellite hints (2.6× slower, entering a cul-de-sac). Removing GPS too degenerates to RECON-like uninformed search, which fails to reach the goal in over 30 min. Goal chaining (merging GPS-intersecting training trajectories into multi-km macro-trajectories) lets the InfoNCE heuristic generalize to km-scale goals even though no training trajectory exceeds 80 m. The hint type shapes behavior: the roadmap-trained model follows roads, while the satellite-trained model cuts across meadows.
method: Latent goal model (VIB): encoder p_φ(z|o_t,o_w) (MobileNet on stacked 160×120 RGB pairs → 64-d Gaussian) and decoder q_θ(a,d,x|z,o_t). The decoder predicts the action (linear/angular velocity), temporal distance, and GPS offset to a waypoint. It is trained by max-likelihood with a KL term to a N(0,I) prior so that sampled z correspond to reachable, collision-free subgoals.

Self-supervised labels from trajectories: pairs of time steps give o_t/o_w, the step count gives distance d, the executed action gives a, and the later GPS reading in the earlier frame gives offset x.

Learned geographic heuristic: p_over(w→G | x_w, x_G, x_t, c_t) with a MobileNet over an overhead image (satellite or roadmap) centered at the robot, concatenated with the GPS triplet, then FC [512,128,32,1]. It is trained with InfoNCE using positives from the same sub-trajectory and negatives from other trajectories; h_over = λ_over(1−p_over), with λ_over=200.

Goal chaining for the heuristic: training trajectories that intersect in 2D (GPS) are merged into multi-km macro-trajectories, and start/end/positive points are sampled from them to supervise long-horizon goals.

ViKiNG-A* physical search: a priority open set of sampled latent waypoints with cost f(w) = g(t,w) + d_Pr[w] + h(w) + v(Pr[w]). The terms are graph shortest path to the parent, the predicted parent→w distance, the learned heuristic, and a visitation-count novelty penalty C·N (C=20). The robot physically drives to the min-cost node, adds the observed image to the topological graph, samples new waypoints, and backtracks naturally.

DriveTo/localization: shortest path on the topological graph, then closed-loop actions from q_θ until the predicted distance is small (close threshold ε=10). Termination occurs when the current image is 'close' to the goal image according to the model.

setting.backbone: MobileNet-based latent goal model (VIB) + MobileNet-based contrastive heuristic network (trained from scratch)
setting.training_data: 42 h of offline real-world robot data: 30 h autonomously collected RECON dataset (>5000 self-supervised trajectories, 9 environments, random-walk collection) + 12 h teleoperation on sidewalks, hiking trails, suburban roads, grasslands and campus. Average trajectory 45 m, none longer than 80 m; overhead satellite/roadmap tiles queried at GPS locations.
setting.observation: monocular forward-facing 170° FoV RGB (160×120) + noisy GPS (2-5 m accuracy) + overhead satellite image or schematic roadmap centered at the current GPS; goal given as an image + approximate GPS
setting.action_space: continuous linear and angular velocity (low-level, from the latent goal model) with high-level selection of sampled latent subgoals on a topological graph
setting.privileged: none (approximate goal GPS and possibly outdated overhead maps are intended inputs; no GT map or pose)

numbers_note: Real-world-only evaluation; no standard benchmark. Table I reports success counts per difficulty bucket (10 trials total), not percentages. The kilometer-scale runs are qualitative single demonstrations with distances only: 1.20 km, 1.55 km, 1.05 km (Fig. 5), a 2.73 km hiking trail with 6 checkpoints (Fig. 6), and a 2.65 km inspection loop with 5 landmarks (Fig. 7). The paper gives two figures for maximum training trajectory length: 'up to 50m' in the heuristic section and 'never longer than 80 meters'.
results: On 10 unseen real-world outdoor goal-seeking trials, ViKiNG reached every goal: 3/3 easy (<50 m), 4/4 medium (50-150 m) and 3/3 hard (150-500 m). The strongest baseline, RECON-H (a RECON variant given GPS and satellite inputs), scored 3/3, 3/4 and 1/3; GCG, offline PPO and BC failed all hard goals. On hard tasks ViKiNG averaged 250.0+ m displacement at 1.36 m/s, versus RECON-H's 188.3 m at 0.41 m/s (over 3× slower). ViKiNG also completed km-scale runs up to about 2.7 km without interventions, despite no training trajectory longer than 80 m.
limitations: Quantitative evaluation is very small (10 trials, 3-4 per difficulty bucket), and ablations and hint-robustness studies are single anecdotal trials; there are no standard benchmarks or simulator comparisons.

Relies on outdoor GPS (2-5 m accuracy) and georeferenced overhead imagery, so it is not directly applicable indoors or in GPS-denied areas; without GPS the search fails to reach the goal within 30 min.

Performs no geometric reconstruction and no optimality guarantees; physical search can enter dead ends and backtrack, and the heuristic is non-admissible and tied to the hint modality it was trained on (a separate model per hint type).
